claim: BRAFV600E mutation is present in over half of all cutaneous melanomas.
source: An activating mutation in the BRAF proto-oncogene (BRAFV600E) drives over half of all cutaneous melanomas (Garnett and Marais, 2004; Davies et al., 2002; Pollock et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: When a melanocyte acquires a BRAFV600E mutation, it usually undergoes clonal proliferation followed by stable arrest resulting in a benign melanocytic nevus.
source: Yet, when a melanocyte acquires a BRAFV600E mutation, the cell does not immediately transform to cancer. Instead, it usually undergoes clonal proliferation followed by stable arrest resulting in a benign skin lesion known as a melanocytic nevus or 'mole' (Pollock et al., 2003; Shain et al., 2015; Bastian, 2014; Dankort et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The BRAFV600E mutation is clonally present in approximately 80% of human melanocytic nevi.
source: The BRAFV600E mutation is clonally present in ~80% of human melanocytic nevi (Pollock et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Melanocyte-specific expression of BRAFV600E is sufficient to induce nevus formation in mice.
source: melanocyte-specific expression of the oncogene is sufficient to induce nevus formation in mice (Dankort et al., 2009; Damsky et al., 2015; Ruiz-Vega et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to published mouse model studies

claim: MIR211-5p, MIR328-3p, MIR125A-5p, and MIR125B-5p are among the top 10 differentially expressed genes elevated in nevi compared to melanomas.
source: Of the differentially expressed genes (adjusted p value<0.05), 6 of the top 10 with elevated expression in nevi were non-coding miRNAs (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1). Among these were miRNAs previously shown as enriched in nevi compared to melanomas, including MIR211-5p, MIR125A-5p, MIR125B-5p, and MIR328-3p (Torres et al., 2020; Latchana et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of RNA sequencing data and referenced in Figure 1B

claim: MIR211-5p, MIR328-3p, and MIR125B-5p are more highly expressed in melanocytic nevi compared to healthy melanocytes or melanomas.
source: Three of the miRNAs (MIR211-5p, MIR328-3p, and MIR125B-5p) were also more highly expressed in melanocytic nevi as compared to healthy melanocytes or melanomas—an expression pattern consistent with enrichment in arrested melanocytes—whereas one miRNA (MIR125A-5p) presented a pattern consistent with lineage-specific expression that is lost upon transformation (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data comparing fresh healthy skin melanocytes, nevus melanocytes, and melanoma melanocytes, shown in Figure 1C

claim: Introduction of MIR211-5p or MIR328-3p into primary human melanocytes results in significantly fewer melanocytes compared to control.
source: The introduction of either MIR211-5p or MIR328-3p resulted in significantly fewer melanocytes compared to a non-targeting control (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data tracking melanocyte proliferation over 7 days after miRNA mimic nucleofection, shown in Figure 1D

claim: Increased concentrations of MIR211-5p or MIR328-3p mimics result in dose-dependent decrease in EdU uptake in melanocytes.
source: Increased concentrations of these mimics resulted in a dose-dependent decrease in EdU uptake, consistent with a cell cycle defect (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 1E

claim: MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p expression in melanocytes does not increase cell death.
source: We observed no evidence of increased cell death (Figure 1H), and confirmed this result with Annexin V staining (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phase imaging cell death counts (Figure 1H) and Annexin V/PI flow cytometry (Figure 1I)

claim: MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p induce proliferation arrest in human melanocytes.
source: Thus, MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p induce proliferation arrest in human melanocytes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations including reduced cell number, decreased EdU uptake, and no increase in cell death

claim: Melanocytes expressing MIR211-5p or MIR328-3p exhibit a 20-40% increase in intracellular dry mass.
source: Further characterization of the QPI images revealed a distinct increase in intra-cellular dry mass in proliferation-arrested conditions (Figure 1K). The dry mass of a cell is a measurement of total biomass (DNA, RNA, proteins, lipids, etc.) and is quantitatively measured by QPI. Relative dry mass fluctuates with cell cycle stage in a predictable manner (Falck Miniotis et al., 2014). The 20–40% increase we observed here is characteristic of cells that have doubled their DNA content but failed to complete mitosis.
evidence: Supported by quantitative phase imaging measurements shown in Figure 1K and interpretation based on published literature

claim: MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p expression in melanocytes results in significant increases of cells with 4N and greater than 4N DNA content.
source: We confirmed this finding by measuring DNA content of the arrested populations (Figure 1L). We observed significant increases of cells with both 4 N DNA content and greater than 4 N DNA content, indicative of cytokinesis failure following DNA replication (Figure 1M).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry DNA content profiling shown in Figures 1L and 1M

claim: Time-lapsed imaging revealed incidences of tripolar mitosis and anaphase bridging in miRNA-expressing melanocytes.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, time-lapsed imaging revealed incidences of tripolar mitosis and anaphase bridging in miRNA-expression melanocytes—both processes associated with cytokinesis failure (Normand and King, 2010)—which were not observed in control conditions or standard culture (Video 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Video 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, with citation to published literature on cytokinesis failure

claim: MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p induce mitotic failure and proliferation arrest when introduced into primary human melanocytes.
source: We conclude that MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p induce mitotic failure and proliferation arrest when introduced into primary human melanocytes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations including DNA content changes, increased dry mass, and observation of mitotic abnormalities

claim: Computationally predicted targets of MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p are enriched in the set of downregulated genes following miRNA nucleofection.
source: As expected, computationally predicted targets of MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p were enriched in the set of downregulated genes following MIR211-5p or MIR328-3p nucleofection, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B

claim: AURKB, GPR3, and MAPKAPK2 showed the greatest magnitude of repression due to miRNA expression with significant EdU reduction upon siRNA-mediated knockdown.
source: AURKB, GPR3, and MAPKAPK2 showed the greatest magnitude of repression due to miRNA expression with significant EdU reduction upon siRNA-mediated knockdown (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by siRNA screen results shown in Figure 2C

claim: AURKB and GPR3 were significantly inhibited upon nucleofection of either MIR211-5p or MIR328-3p.
source: Of these, AURKB (predicted MIR211-5p target) and GPR3 (predicted MIR328-3p target) were significantly inhibited upon nucleofection of either miRNA (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by gene expression measurements after miRNA nucleofection shown in Figure 2D

claim: The AURKB transcript contains a potential MIR328-3p binding site just before the 3′ untranslated region.
source: Further exploration of the AURKB transcript revealed a potential MIR328-3p binding site just before the 3′ untranslated region (Figure 2E; Dweep et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by computational prediction shown in Figure 2E and citation to prediction tool

claim: No candidate MIR211-5p binding site was identified in the GPR3 transcript.
source: In contrast, we were unable to identify a candidate MIR211-5p binding site in the GPR3 transcript, suggesting indirect inhibition of this gene by MIR211-5p.
evidence: Based on computational analysis and inference about mechanism

claim: AURKB and GPR3 protein and mRNA expression is enriched in melanomas compared to nevi.
source: The expression of both AURKB and GPR3 protein and mRNA was enriched in melanomas as compared to nevi (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining and RNA sequencing data from clinical specimens shown in Figures 2G and 2H

claim: Expression of AURKB partially rescues both MIR211-5p-induced and MIR328-3p-induced arrest in melanocytes.
source: Expression of either mRNA partially rescued MIR211-5p-induced arrest, while AURKB, but not GPR3, partially rescued MIR328-3p-induced arrest (Figure 2L).
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation experiments with lentiviral overexpression shown in Figure 2L

claim: AURKB inhibition is a critical convergent node of both MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p in facilitating proliferation arrest in nevi.
source: Thus, while other MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p targets, including GPR3, may play a role in the induction of melanocyte proliferation arrest, these data suggest that AURKB inhibition is a critical convergent node of both miRNAs in facilitating proliferation arrest in nevi.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from rescue experiments and supported by the known role of AURKB in mitosis

claim: BRAFV600E expression in primary human melanocytes results in an accumulation of cells with ≥4N DNA content and a decrease in cells with 2N DNA content.
source: Cell cycle profiling confirmed a significant and dose-dependent accumulation of cells with ≥4 N DNA content and a decrease in cells with 2 N DNA content (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry DNA content profiling shown in Figures 3D and 3E

claim: Relative per cell dry mass increases by 50% concurrent with BRAFV600E-induced arrest in melanocytes.
source: Similar to our observations for miRNA-induced arrest, relative per cell dry mass increased by 50% concurrent with BRAFV600E induced-arrest (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phase imaging measurements shown in Figure 3C

claim: The cell cycle profile of BRAFV600E-arrested melanocytes is dissimilar to that of melanocytes treated with CDK4/6 inhibitor PD0332991.
source: The cell cycle profiles were notably dissimilar to that of melanocytes treated with a pharmacologic CDK4/6 inhibitor (PD0332991, Palbociclib) (Clark et al., 2016) known to induce G0/G1 arrest.
evidence: Supported by comparison of DNA content profiles and citation to published literature on the inhibitor

claim: Treatment with AURKB inhibitor AZD2811 results in an accumulation of melanocytes with ≥4N DNA content and a decrease in cells with 2N DNA content.
source: Treatment with a pharmacologic AURKB inhibitor (AZD2811, Barasertib) (Helfrich et al., 2016) that induces G2/M arrest and mitotic failure also resulted in an accumulation of melanocytes with ≥4 N DNA content and a decrease in cells with 2 N DNA content.
evidence: Supported by DNA content profiling data and citation to published literature on the inhibitor

claim: BRAFV600E-induced proliferation arrest in melanocytes is reversible and dependent on continued oncogene expression.
source: Within 12 hr of doxycycline removal, the previously arrested melanocytes began to proliferate (Figure 3F), demonstrating that BRAFV600E-induced proliferation arrest in melanocytes is reversible and dependent on continued oncogene expression.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data showing resumption of proliferation after doxycycline removal, shown in Figure 3F

claim: In the presence of TPA, BRAFV600E expression inhibits melanocyte proliferation.
source: In the presence of TPA, BRAFV600E expression inhibited cell proliferation.
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation experiments under different media conditions shown in Figure 3G

claim: In TPA-free media, BRAFV600E expression induces melanocyte proliferation.
source: By contrast, in TPA-free media, BRAFV600E expression induced proliferation, a phenotype that persisted for the remaining duration of the primary cultures (4–6 weeks).
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation experiments under different media conditions shown in Figure 3G

claim: Melanocytes exposed to high concentration of doxycycline (60 ng/ml) for 30 days in +TPA media remain arrested for the duration of doxycycline treatment then grow again upon removal of either doxycycline or TPA.
source: Melanocytes in +TPA media remained arrested for the duration of doxycycline treatment then grew again upon removal of either doxycycline or TPA (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: Supported by long-term time-lapse imaging data shown in Figures 3J and 3K

claim: BRAFV600E expression induces divergent and interconvertible phenotypes—either hyperproliferation or reversible arrest—in human melanocytes conditional on extrinsic stimuli.
source: From these results, we conclude that BRAFV600E expression induces divergent and interconvertible phenotypes—either hyperproliferation or a reversible arrest—in human melanocytes conditional on extrinsic stimuli.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing different phenotypes under different media conditions

claim: MIR328-3p expression is relatively stable with less than twofold changes across TPA and BRAFV600E conditions.
source: The expression of MIR328-3p was relatively stable, demonstrating less than twofold changes across conditions (Figure 4A–B, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figures 4A and 4B

claim: MIR211-5p is one of the most differentially expressed genes in +TPA conditions compared to TPA-free conditions.
source: In contrast, MIR211-5p was one of the most differentially expressed genes in +TPA conditions compared to TPA-free conditions (adj. p=6.8E−23) (Figure 4A–B, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by small RNA sequencing differential expression analysis shown in Figures 4A and 4B

claim: Induction of BRAFV600E in +TPA conditions does not alter expression of MIR211-5p or MIR328-3p.
source: Induction of BRAFV600E in +TPA conditions did not further alter expression of either miRNA.
evidence: Supported by small RNA sequencing data comparing conditions with and without doxycycline

claim: MIR211-5p is the most significantly downregulated miRNA when comparing arrested melanocytes in +TPA +Dox conditions to proliferative melanocytes in −TPA +Dox conditions.
source: Direct comparison of the arrested melanocytes in +TPA +Dox conditions to the proliferative melanocytes in −TPA +Dox conditions revealed MIR211-5p as the most significantly downregulated miRNA in the proliferative condition (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: The addition of doxycycline induces AURKB expression in TPA-free/MIR211-5p low conditions, but not in +TPA/MIR211-5p high conditions.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the addition of doxycycline induced AURKB expression in TPA-free/MIR211-5p low conditions, but this effect was not observed in +TPA/MIR211-5p high conditions (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data showing AURKB expression levels under different conditions, shown in Figure 4E

claim: 97.4% of the variance between mRNA samples is explained by two principal components—PC1 (81.75% variance) separates transcriptomes based on TPA exposure and PC2 (15.7% variance) separates transcriptomes based on BRAFV600E expression.
source: Principal component (PC) analysis revealed that 97.4 % of the variance between samples was explained by two PCs—PC1 (81.75 variance) separated transcriptomes based upon exposure to TPA and PC2 (15.7% variance) separated transcriptomes based upon BRAFV600E expression (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by principal component analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Gene sets uniquely enriched in +TPA media include signatures associated with cell cycle regulation, G2-M checkpoint, oxidative phosphorylation, the MITF program, and differentiated melanocytes.
source: Gene sets uniquely enriched in +TPA media included signatures associated with cell cycle regulation, such as the G2-M checkpoint, oxidative phosphorylation, the MITF program, and differentiated melanocytes.
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4F

claim: TPA-free media-induced gene sets are associated with cell adhesion and melanocyte progenitor and stem cells.
source: In contrast, TPA-free media-induced gene sets are associated with cell adhesion and melanocyte progenitor and stem cells.
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Melanocytes grown in TPA-free media express higher levels of AXL and lower levels of MLANA compared to those grown in +TPA media.
source: Corroborating this observation, melanocytes grown in TPA-free media expressed higher levels of AXL (Figure 4G–H), lower levels of MLANA, a melanocyte differentiation marker
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 4G and 4H

claim: Melanocytes grown in TPA-free media present greater activity of aldehyde dehydrogenase compared to those grown in +TPA media.
source: and presented greater activity of aldehyde dehydrogenase, enzymatic activity associated with stemness (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by ALDEFLUOR assay data shown in Figure 4I

claim: Exposure to TPA induces a more differentiated melanocyte phenotype.
source: These results indicate that exposure to TPA induces a more differentiated melanocyte phenotype, consistent with previous reports (Prince et al., 2003; Vidács et al., 2021; Kormos et al., 2011).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from gene expression and protein marker data, supported by citations to published literature

claim: AURKB expression rescues BRAFV600E-induced arrest in melanocytes grown in +TPA conditions.
source: AURKB expression had no baseline effect on melanocyte growth, but rescued BRAFV600E-induced arrest (Figure 4L)
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation experiments with lentiviral AURKB overexpression shown in Figure 4L

claim: Sponges against either MIR211-5p or MIR328-3p increase baseline division rate and rescue BRAFV600E-induced arrest in melanocytes.
source: Also consistent with the model, sponges against either MIR211-5p or MIR328-3p increased baseline division rate and rescued BRAFV600E-induced arrest, demonstrating that both miRNAs contribute to inhibition of melanocyte division, with effects that are more pronounced in the presence of growth signals.
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation experiments with miRNA sponge constructs shown in Figure 4L

claim: All nevi within a cohort of 15 exhibited binucleation.
source: Histopathologic analysis revealed that all nevi within the cohort exhibited binucleation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by histopathologic examination of clinical specimens shown in Figure 5A

claim: The percent of binucleated melanocytes in nevi ranged from 3% to 12% with a mean of 6.3%.
source: The percent observed binucleated melanocytes ranged from 3% to 12% (mean=6.3%).
evidence: Supported by quantification of histopathologic analysis

claim: Giant multinucleated cells were observed in 10 of 15 nevi.
source: We also observed giant multinucleated cells in 10 of the 15 nevi, indicative of multiple rounds of DNA synthesis and cytokinetic failure and consistent with previous reports (Rogers et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by histopathologic examination and citation to published literature

claim: Nevus-derived melanocytes frequently contain 4N and 8N DNA content.
source: Consistent with the histopathologic cohort, co-staining with melanocyte marker, MLANA, and Hoechst revealed frequent 4 N and 8 N melanocytes (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and DNA staining of cultured nevus melanocytes shown in Figure 5C

claim: mCherry positive nevus melanocytes (expressing AURKB) divide significantly more than their mCherry negative counterparts.
source: Transduction of nevus melanocytes with an AURKB and mCherry expressing lentiviral vector at low multiplicity of infection showed that the mCherry positive cells divided significantly more than their mCherry negative counterparts (Figure 5D–E) in cells from all three nevus donors.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging tracking cell division shown in Figures 5D and 5E

claim: Expression of AURKB is rate limiting for the proliferation of human nevus melanocytes.
source: This result suggests that expression of AURKB is also rate limiting for the proliferation of human nevus melanocytes, as we observed in primary melanocytes expressing BRAFV600E.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from rescue experiments in nevus melanocytes

claim: Primary human melanocytes are largely resistant to AURKB inhibitor Barasertib with reduced growth apparent only at supraphysiological levels.
source: Primary melanocytes were largely resistant to the compound with reduced growth apparent only at supraphysiological levels (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by dose-response growth rate measurements shown in Figure 5F

claim: BRAFV600E melanoma cultures respond to tenfold lower dosage of Barasertib compared to primary melanocytes with GR50 approaching zero.
source: In contrast, both melanoma cultures responded to tenfold lower dosage of the compound with GR50 approaching zero, indicating primarily arrest, not death.
evidence: Supported by dose-response growth rate measurements shown in Figure 5F

claim: Per cell dry mass of melanoma cells increases significantly upon Barasertib treatment, consistent with G2/M arrest.
source: In these conditions, the per cell dry mass also increased significantly, consistent with a G2/M arrest (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phase imaging measurements shown in Figure 5G

claim: AURKB inhibition limits the rate of BRAFV600E-induced proliferation in human melanocytic nevi and melanomas.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that AURKB inhibition limits the rate of BRAFV600E-induced proliferation in human melanocytic nevi and melanomas.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from rescue experiments in nevus melanocytes and drug sensitivity experiments in melanoma cells

claim: Recent observations have challenged the role of oncogene-induced senescence in melanocytic nevus formation.
source: Recent observations have challenged the role of oncogene-induced senescence in melanocytic nevus formation, necessitating investigations into alternative mechanisms for the establishment and maintenance of proliferation arrest in nevi.
evidence: Statement about the current state of the field

claim: MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p induce mitotic failure, genome duplication, and proliferation arrest in human melanocytes through convergent targeting of AURKB.
source: Two of these microRNAs—MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p—induced mitotic failure, genome duplication, and proliferation arrest in human melanocytes through convergent targeting of AURKB.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from multiple experiments

claim: BRAFV600E induces a reversible and conditional proliferation arrest in primary human melanocytes.
source: We demonstrate that BRAFV600E induces a similar proliferation arrest in primary human melanocytes that is both reversible and conditional.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from multiple experiments

claim: BRAFV600E expression stimulates either arrest or proliferation depending on the differentiation state of the melanocyte.
source: Specifically, BRAFV600E expression stimulates either arrest or proliferation depending on the differentiation state of the melanocyte.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from experiments with different media conditions

claim: Genome duplication occurs in human melanocytic nevi.
source: We report genome duplication in human melanocytic nevi
evidence: Supported by DNA content profiling and histopathologic analysis of clinical specimens

claim: AURKB and microRNAs show reciprocal expression in nevi and melanomas.
source: reciprocal expression of AURKB and microRNAs in nevi and melanomas
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing and immunohistochemistry data from clinical specimens

claim: Arrested human nevus cells can be rescued with AURKB expression.
source: and rescue of arrested human nevus cells with AURKB expression.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing increased division in AURKB-expressing nevus melanocytes

claim: The prevailing theory to explain BRAFV600E's role in nevus formation is oncogene-induced senescence.
source: The prevailing theory to explain this seemingly paradoxical role for BRAFV600E is oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) (Michaloglou et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement about the current paradigm in the field with citation

claim: Cellular senescence is defined as the permanent cell-cycle arrest of previously replication-competent cells.
source: Cellular senescence is defined as the permanent cell-cycle arrest of previously replication-competent cells (He and Sharpless, 2017; Roy et al., 2020).
evidence: Definition supported by citations to published literature

claim: Senescence is associated with elevated expression of p16INK4A, cyclin-dependent-kinase inhibitors, TP53, H2AX, lysosomal beta-galactosidase, senescence-associated secretory proteins, and a DNA content profile indicative of arrest in G0/G1 phases.
source: Senescence is associated with a variety of molecular hallmarks including elevated expression of p16INK4A and other cyclin-dependent-kinase inhibitors, TP53, H2AX, lysosomal beta-galactosidase and senescence-associated secretory proteins (SASPs) as well as a DNA content profile indicative of arrest in the G0/G1 phases of the cell cycle (Roy et al., 2020; Serrano et al., 1997; Campisi and d'Adda di Fagagna, 2007; Collado and Serrano, 2006; Afshari et al., 1993; Chatsirisupachai et al., 2019).
evidence: Description of senescence markers supported by multiple citations

claim: The concept of OIS as a barrier to tumorigenesis derived from observations of durable proliferation arrest induced by overexpression of oncogenic RAS or RAF in immortalized human fibroblasts.
source: The concept of OIS as a barrier to tumorigenesis derived from observations of a durable proliferation arrest induced by overexpression of oncogenic RAS or RAF in immortalized human fibroblasts (Serrano et al., 1997; Zhu et al., 1998).
evidence: Historical context supported by citations to seminal papers

claim: Cell cycle re-entry accompanies nevus recurrence, eruption, or transformation to primary melanoma.
source: Cell cycle re-entry that accompanies nevus recurrence (King et al., 2009), eruption (Burian and Jemec, 2019), or transformation to primary melanoma suggests that the nevus arrest phenotype is reversible rather than permanent.
evidence: Clinical observations supported by citations to published literature

claim: Expression of senescence markers does not readily distinguish human melanocytic nevi from primary or transformed melanocytes in humans or mice.
source: Similarly, the expression of senescence markers does not readily distinguish human melanocytic nevi from primary or transformed melanocytes in humans (16INK4A, TP53, H2AX, and beta-galactosidase) or mice (any known hallmark of senescence) (Ruiz-Vega et al., 2020; Cotter et al., 2007; Tran et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: p16INK4A expression is neither ubiquitous across melanocytic nevi, nor uniform within the cells of a single nevus.
source: Despite this, p16INK4A expression is neither ubiquitous across melanocytic nevi, nor uniform within the cells of a single nevus (Oaxaca et al., 2020; Zeng et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Neither knockdown of the p16INK4A transcript nor ablation of the CDKN2A locus prevents the onset or rescues BRAFV600E-induced proliferation arrest.
source: and neither knockdown of the 16INK4A transcript nor ablation of the CDKN2A locus prevents the onset or rescues BRAFV600E-induced proliferation arrest (Michaloglou et al., 2005; Zeng et al., 2018; Haferkamp et al., 2009; McNeal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published experimental studies

claim: BRAFV600E stimulates expression of p15INK4B, the translational product of the CDKN2B gene.
source: BRAFV600E also stimulates expression of p15INK4B—the translational product of the CDKN2B gene (McNeal et al., 2015) which is situated adjacent to the CDKN2A locus
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Selection against the CDKN2A/B locus occurs after BRAFV600E melanocytes have already escaped nevus-associated arrest.
source: While the loss of the CDKN2A/B locus is a formative event in melanoma progression, genetic evolution studies of melanoma progression suggest that selection against the CDKN2A/B locus occurs after BRAFV600E melanocytes have already escaped nevus-associated arrest (Zeng et al., 2018; Shain et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to genetic evolution studies

claim: MIR211-5p expression levels classify nevi from melanomas with a high degree of accuracy.
source: Indeed, MIR211-5p expression levels classify nevi from melanomas with a high degree of accuracy (Babapoor et al., 2016; Torres et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published diagnostic studies

claim: AURKB expression was previously reported as significantly elevated in melanoma metastases.
source: AURKB expression was previously reported as significantly elevated in melanoma metastases (Sharma et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Reentry of cells into cell cycle after mitotic failure causes genome duplication and accumulation of copy number alterations in other cancers.
source: In melanoma, the specific cause of this genomic instability is unknown, but reentry of cells into cell cycle after mitotic failure has been shown to cause genome duplication and accumulation of copy number alterations in other cancers (Telentschak et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study in other cancer types

claim: Mitotic failure serves as a barrier to melanoma progression.
source: These data suggest that mitotic failure serves as a barrier to melanoma progression and is consistent with the genome duplication and copy number alterations associated with invasive melanoma (Shain et al., 2015; Vergara et al., 2021).
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data and supported by citations to published studies on melanoma genomics

claim: Nevus eruption has been observed in metastatic melanoma patients treated with single agent selective BRAF inhibitors.
source: Interestingly, nevus eruption has been observed in metastatic melanoma patients treated with single agent selective BRAF inhibitors (Cohen et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014; Chu et al., 2012; Dalle et al., 2013; Zimmer et al., 2012)
evidence: Clinical observation supported by multiple citations

claim: Loss of MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p expression and restoration of AURKB expression is concurrent with progression to melanoma.
source: Since our data suggest that loss of MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p expression and restoration of AURKB expression is concurrent with progression to melanoma
evidence: Conclusion drawn from expression profiling data in clinical specimens

claim: MIR211-5p is reported to be transcriptionally regulated by both MITF and UV exposure.
source: MIR211-5p is reported to be transcriptionally regulated by both MITF (Mazar et al., 2010) and UV exposure (Su et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: TPA-free media containing endothelin-1 did not elicit MIR211-5p expression or BRAFV600E arrest.
source: However, TPA-free media containing an endothelin receptor type B ligand, endothelin-1, did not elicit MIR211-5p expression or BRAFV600E arrest, suggestive that the downstream signaling pathways regulated by the two molecules are not identical.
evidence: Experimental observation leading to inference about signaling pathways

claim: PKC activation can result in increased MAPK signaling.
source: PKC activation can also result in increased MAPK signaling (Herrera et al., 1998; Ueda et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The term 'mitogenic window' describes the specific range of oncogene doses that elicit a hyperproliferative phenotype.
source: The term 'mitogenic window' describes the specific range of oncogene doses that elicit a hyperproliferative phenotype.
evidence: Definition of a known concept in the field

claim: In TPA conditions, the mitogenic window for BRAFV600E expression is exceedingly narrow.
source: Regardless, our data demonstrate that in TPA conditions the mitogenic window for BRAFV600E expression is, at least, exceedingly narrow
evidence: Conclusion drawn from dose-response experiments

claim: In non-TPA conditions, the mitogenic window for BRAFV600E expression is wide open.
source: whereas in non-TPA conditions the window is wide open.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from dose-response experiments

claim: Dysregulation of the spindle checkpoint in nevi may contribute directly to the copy number variations present in melanomas.
source: Further experiments will be necessary to determine whether dysregulation of the spindle checkpoint in nevi contributes directly to the copy number variations present in melanomas.
evidence: Speculative statement about future research directions

claim: The arrest response of human melanocytes to BRAFV600E is distinct from BRAFV600E-induced OIS in other cell types.
source: Given these observations, we reasoned that the arrest response of human melanocytes to BRAFV600E might be distinct from previous reports of BRAFV600E-induced OIS in other cell types.
evidence: Hypothesis based on review of literature and preliminary observations

claim: Nevus-associated arrest is conditional and coordinated by reversible changes in gene expression.
source: Specifically, we hypothesized that nevus-associated arrest is conditional and coordinated by reversible changes in gene expression.
evidence: Hypothesis stated by the authors

claim: Regulation of miRNAs coupled to differentiation status permits toggling between BRAFV600E-driven hyperproliferative to arrested phenotypes in melanocytes.
source: Merging these two observations, we discover that in melanocytes, regulation of miRNAs coupled to differentiation status permits toggling between BRAFV600E-driven hyperproliferative to arrested phenotypes.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations

claim: The mechanisms governing whether BRAFV600E induces arrest or proliferation are a function of the cell's transcriptional state rather than directly downstream of BRAFV600E itself.
source: While MIR328-3p downregulation likely contributes to increased proliferation in this condition, the more pronounced effect of TPA on MIR211-5p expression suggests that the mechanisms governing whether BRAFV600E induces arrest or proliferation are a function of the cell's transcriptional state rather than directly downstream of BRAFV600E itself.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from transcriptomic analysis comparing effects of TPA and BRAFV600E

claim: MIR211-5p expression in +TPA conditions dampens AURKB activation by BRAFV600E.
source: We therefore reasoned that MIR211-5p expression in +TPA conditions might dampen AURKB activation by BRAFV600E. Consistent with this hypothesis, the addition of doxycycline induced AURKB expression in TPA-free/MIR211-5p low conditions, but this effect was not observed in +TPA/MIR211-5p high conditions (Figure 4E).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4E

claim: miRNA function depends on the expression level of its targets.
source: However, as inhibitors of translation, miRNA function depends on the expression level of its targets (Mukherji et al., 2011; Ovando-Vázquez et al., 2016), effectively functioning as buffers of gene expression that prevent aberrantly high levels of a transcript (Ebert and Sharp, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on miRNA function

claim: BRAFV600E has been previously demonstrated as an upstream activator of AURKB transcription in melanoma cells.
source: BRAFV600E has been previously demonstrated as an upstream activator of AURKB transcription in melanoma cells (Sharma et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: The inability of BRAFV600E to induce AURKB in +TPA context serves as a bottleneck in cell division.
source: AURKB expression had no baseline effect on melanocyte growth, but rescued BRAFV600E-induced arrest (Figure 4L), suggesting the inability of the oncogene to induce AURKB in this context serves as a bottleneck in cell division.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from rescue experiments shown in Figure 4L

claim: Both MIR211-5p and MIR328-3p contribute to inhibition of melanocyte division, with effects that are more pronounced in the presence of growth signals.
source: Also consistent with the model, sponges against either MIR211-5p or MIR328-3p increased baseline division rate and rescued BRAFV600E-induced arrest, demonstrating that both miRNAs contribute to inhibition of melanocyte division, with effects that are more pronounced in the presence of growth signals.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from miRNA sponge experiments

claim: 3-12% binucleation in nevi is likely an underestimate because binucleation can only be observed in cells sectioned perpendicular to the plane of adjacent nuclei.
source: It is important to note that since binucleation can only be observed in the fraction of cells sectioned perpendicular to the plane of the adjacent nuclei, 3–12% is likely an underestimate.
evidence: Inference based on technical limitations of histological sectioning

claim: The data describe an alternative molecular mechanism for melanocytic nevus formation that is congruent with both experimental and clinical observations.
source: Taken together, our data describe an alternative molecular mechanism for melanocytic nevus formation that is congruent with both experimental and clinical observations.
evidence: Summary statement of the overall findings and their significance
